Directed transition graphs offer evidence beyond textual similarity. GLSRec (2026) combines global transitions across users with local sequence modeling; [Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209) uses a directed weighted projection of user–item interactions for complementary recommendation. [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02130) emphasizes that complements combine relevance with dissimilarity, using low- and mid-frequency graph filters. Thus, smoothing every connected item toward similar embeddings can discard useful distinctions.

Text need not require external pretrained weights: [Sceptre (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.08839) jointly learns textual topics and product-link predictors. However, its supervised relationship labels and review-rich inputs exceed this task’s available evidence. A feasible adaptation—not a published result—is sparse title/description TF–IDF or trainable bag-of-token embeddings, with separate source/target projections trained on observed next-item transitions. These transitions provide directional supervision but cannot establish whether a pair is a substitute or complement; text similarity alone cannot establish compatibility either.

A [2026 benchmark audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07125) finds that retrieving from a few-hop transition graph using the latest one or two items, then ranking by feature similarity, can rival sophisticated recommenders, including on Amazon CDs. This supports testing an inexpensive transition-plus-text residual alongside SASRec. Build edges only from training histories; compare transition-only, text-only, and combined scores using the common macro validation HR@10. The audit’s results do not establish gains under this pinned evaluator or guarantee that its feature pipeline meets the no-pretrained-weights constraint.
